records.title: Bobbi Brown Teaches Makeup and Beauty course
records.content:
Lesson Plan

  1. Bobbi’s Beauty Philosophy
    06:32
    Bobbi shares her beauty philosophy: Makeup should be quick and natural, and it should enhance who you are. She explains what her class will cover and why she’ll be demonstrating on models of different ages and with a range of skin tones.
  1. The Changing Face of Beauty
    7:37
    While makeup has been around for ages, styles are constantly changing. Bobbi discusses makeup from the 1960s to today. She talks about the origin of Bobbi Brown Cosmetics and how the face of beauty has changed through the “It” girls of the times.
  1. Color and Makeup
    8:38
    Color is critical: It can make a statement and reveal your individuality. Bobbi discusses how color and style are key to self-expression and how undertones can help you find the right colors. She also clears up a misconception about nude makeup.
  1. Inside Bobbi’s Makeup Kit
    7:14
    Bobbi shares the essential items in her day bag, her evening bag, and her travel bag. You’ll learn how to simplify your makeup collection and carry only the essentials for different moments of your day and life.
  1. Foundation
    31:18
    Demonstrating on models with different skin tones, Bobbi shows you techniques for applying your foundation.
  1. Using Tinted Moisturizer
    5:04
    When you don’t need a full face of foundation, you can use a tinted moisturizer instead. Demonstrating on a medium skin tone, Bobbi applies tinted moisturizer and shows how you can then use your foundation and concealer for touch-ups, creating a spotless look with a healthy glow.
  1. Bronzer and Blush
    24:02
    These are Bobbi’s favorite products because they can make you look great when you’re not feeling your best. Bobbi applies bronzer and blush to three models and discusses the tools, techniques, and products used.
  1. Eyes and Brows
    26:57
    Bobbi demonstrates how to play up your eyes and correctly fill in your brows. You’ll learn Bobbi’s tips and tricks for the eye and brow area, including which mascara color is the only one you should use.
  1. Creating a Statement Lip
    8:56
    Demonstrating with a dark matte color, Bobbi applies a statement lip on a model and shares how you can do it, too. This application works for a classic red, a bright pink, or darker and more unforgiving colors.
  1. Skincare Essentials
    13:26
    Bobbi breaks down today’s skincare products, from makeup removers to moisturizers, and explains which products are essential for healthy skin.
  1. Workplace Makeup
    8:59
    As an entrepreneur and CEO, Bobbi knows how to play up her features for the workplace while still looking professional. She’ll show you how to apply a workplace-appropriate look, depending on the type of office you work in.
  1. Self-Application: Day to Night
    12:56
    So you can learn to be your own best makeup artist, Bobbi talks a model through how to apply her own makeup, emphasizing how to choose the right colors.
  1. The Perfect Smoky Eye
    17:20
    The smoky eye is a technique that can easily go wrong. Bobbi shows you how to apply a simple, modern smoky eye and then shows how you can play it up.
  1. 1-Minute Makeup
    2:49
    As a working artist and businesswoman, Bobbi knows how important it is to be able to do your makeup in just about a minute. She demonstrates a quick and easy look that uses only a few products.
  1. Makeup Mistakes
    7:19
    Bobbi discusses some common makeup mistakes—including using too light of a foundation and washing out the color of your lips—and does a live demonstration of how to fix them.
  1. For Aspiring Makeup Artists
    11:27
    Bobbi shares personal stories and lessons from her career as a makeup artist.
  1. Editorial Makeup
    18:03
    Bobbi shows you how to experiment with bold colors and not be afraid to make mistakes or take a look too far.
  1. Conclusion
    02:08
    Bobbi shares lessons from her decades in the beauty industry: Be on time, ask for help, and do the most you can for others. She believes in the power of hard work and determination and urges you to not give up on your passions and goals.
  1. Bonus: Bobbi’s Business Philosophy
    8:04
    Bobbi discusses the business of beauty and offers advice for aspiring leaders. She shares lessons from her time in the boardroom, from building a team to giving a business time to grow.

records.title: Communicate with emotional intelligence
records.content:
Transcript

Communicating with emotional intelligence can propel your career to the next level. Emotionally intelligent communicators boost bottom line performance of their organizations. They build great relationships and they win bonuses. Hello, I'm Brenda Bailey-Hughes. I teach emotionally intelligent communication at a nationally ranked business school. And I use the content from this course when I coach business professionals and executives like yourself. I'm so glad you're joining me to learn things like how do you keep a poker face when inside your upset? How do you read a room to know what people are really thinking? How to respond when someone else is angry or sad. And, how do you show empathy? At the end of the course, test your EI savvy by spotting do's and don'ts in a scenario. I know you're smart, but at the end of the day, your emotional quotient, or EQ, can help you more than your IQ. Your EQ will further your career. So let's get started.

records.title: x Learn Emotional Intelligence, the Key Determiner of Success course
What is emotional intelligence?
records.content:
Transcript

- Two people interview for an internal position. Someone on the interview committee says they seem about the same on paper, but, I vote for Zara, she's great to work with. Another interviewer says she knows people all over the company and those relationships can help us. Another said yeah, during the interview, Zara nailed the question when we asked about weaknesses. She knows where she's going to struggle and I appreciate that honesty. Zara got the job because of her emotional intelligence. She has a high EQ, or emotional quotient. The Institute for Health and Human Potential defines emotional intelligence as being aware that emotions can drive behavior and impact people, positively or negatively. And it's learning how to manage those emotions, both our own and others, especially when we are under pressure. I like the way author Travis Bradberry puts it. Emotional intelligence is the other kind of smart. We all know that person, or maybe we are that person, who's talented, smart, but just doesn't seem to get people. Or maybe it's someone that's moody, has a bad temper. These folks maybe have intelligence and technical skills, which are important, but those are threshold capabilities. Skills that get us in the door or into entry level spots. EQ, your emotional quotient, now that's your differentiator. Emotional intelligence is composed of four categories. Self-awareness. A colleague recently turned down a promotion because he values being in the classroom. The promotion would have meant less student contact. He said, I know what I'm good at, and administration is not it. The only motivator for me to take that job was ego, and that's a terrible reason. This is self-awareness. Know your talents, know your weaknesses and be honest about your motivation. The second category is self-regulation. Our ability to manage our lives and our emotions. Third, empathy. Empathy is understanding another's perspective and feelings. With empathy, we recognize how decisions get made and who the influencers are. One of my coaching clients received a bad client review for his entire department. I asked what are the top three things you can do to get a better review? He told me his three ideas, and then I asked what would be the top three things if I asked your client? He sat very quietly for a moment and then he said, oh, they're not the same things at all. Knowing that his own perspective was different than the client, empathizing was the first step in rebuilding trust with that customer. And finally, relationship management. Relationship management involves meeting diverse people, creating and nurturing connections and being available to help one another. You can build your emotional quotient by making an effort to meet people from all over your organization, your industry, and beyond. Don't just exchange business cards and forget these acquaintances. Nurture the ties to the point that you influence and support one another. Memorize these four components of emotional intelligence, and then start some detective work. Look for great examples of emotional intelligence around you. Notice the people who demonstrate self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy and relationship management. They can become your mentors as you increase your own emotional quotient.

Brenda Bailey-Hughes

records.title: Why emotional intelligence matters
records.content:
I do some communication coaching for an accounting firm. Before I worked with them, they had already done in-depth emotional intelligence training with every one of their partners. I'm loving this approach, so I asked why did you focus on emotional intelligence? And you know what they said? Because of the research that backs emotional intelligence. Research like this. Emotional intelligence boosts the bottom line performance of your organization and wins bonuses for you. Study after study shows a positive and significant relationship between EI and job performance. Whether you're studying healthcare workers, accountants, students or office workers, emotional intelligence enhances job performance. In one study of a global food and beverage company, researcher, David McClelland, found that when senior managers had a critical mass of EI capabilities, their divisions outperformed yearly earning goals by 20%. And that resulted in them being awarded nice bonuses. In contrast execs who lacked EI, were rarely rated as outstanding in their reviews. Customer interaction demands emotional intelligence. My husband and I went out to eat one night and we watched as the manager berated a waiter for some mistake he'd made. We left without ordering, and we've never been back. We're not alone. Customers despise emotional outburst, even if it's not directed at them. Research by Porath and Pearson shows that people are less likely to buy from a company with an employee that is perceived as rude, whether that rudeness is directed at them or at other employees. So the research starts to stack up. But does EQ count as much as IQ or technical skills? In research at an accounting firm, the partners with really strong analytical abilities added 50% more incremental profit than partners with less analytical skill. So that's not bad. But the partners with high social skills, that's EI, they added 110% more incremental profit. A lack of emotional intelligence can be a career roadblock for you. The Center for Creative Leadership estimates that 75% of careers are derailed for reasons related to emotional competencies. Building your emotional intelligence is the surest way I know of growing your career's success. So how strong do you think your EI skills are? As you think about that, know that people tend to overestimate their EI strength. We may not be quite as good at EI as we think we are, but this course is your chance to enhance your emotional quotient and unleash your success.

Brenda Bailey-Hughes
